summary: Ages 8-9 applied place-value problem-solving: children choose and justify a place-value strategy (rounding, comparing, ordering, flexible partitioning) to solve rich, multi-step, real-context problems with increasingly large numbers (populations, distances, prices). This is a META topic — the learning target is deliberate strategy selection and using rounding to check reasonableness, not first-time acquisition of the four-digit toolkit.
misconceptions: Reaching for a memorised procedure without checking it fits the problem.
Rounding at the wrong stage or to an unhelpful accuracy.
Comparing/ordering errors carried into problem contexts (multi-zero, mixed length).
Not sense-checking an answer against an estimate.
Losing place-value meaning when numbers get large or contextual.

activities.title: The large-number problem studio
steps: Read a real-context problem such as: four cities have populations 53,847, 48,206, 51,330 and 49,975 — order them from largest to smallest and estimate the total.

Choose which place-value tool fits the task before computing: a number line (for rounding/estimating), an ordering rail (for comparing/ordering), a bar model (for multi-step structure) or a place-value chart (for partitioning).
Act with the chosen tool — e.g. place each population on the ordering rail, then round each to the nearest thousand on the number line and add the rounded values to estimate the total.
State aloud or in writing WHY that tool fit this problem, referencing place value.
Compute the exact answer and compare it against your rounded estimate to check reasonableness.
activities.insight: The right place-value move depends on what the problem asks; rounding gives a fast estimate that you can use to sense-check an exact answer.

activities.title: Mixed problem set with strategy matching
steps: Work through varied items: multi-step word problems, 'which is larger / best estimate' choices, estimate-then-check tasks, and fill-in-the-blank computations.
For each item, match the problem to the place-value strategy that fits it (round, compare, order, partition) before solving.
Estimate first using rounding, then compute and confirm the estimate was reasonable.
activities.insight: Different problem shapes call for different place-value moves; recognising the shape is the first step to solving it.

activities.title: 'How did you decide?' strategy dialogue
steps: Respond to a real-figure puzzle posed by a partner or teacher (e.g. 'about how many people live in these two towns together?').
Explain which place-value move you chose and why — did you round, compare, or order, and to what accuracy?
Answer probing follow-ups about your choice of accuracy.
activities.insight: Justifying a strategy out loud makes strategy selection deliberate and reveals whether the degree of rounding fits the purpose.

activities.title: Diagnostic: is 'about 54,000' fair?
steps: Consider: a news report says a football crowd was 'about 54,000'; the exact number counted was 53,847.
Decide whether 'about 54,000' is a fair thing to report or wrong because it isn't exact, and explain how you'd decide when a rounded number is good enough.
Compare candidate estimates against 53,847 — is 'about 54,000' closer than 'about 50,000'? Which would be more useful for a news report, and why?
activities.insight: A sensibly rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer; how much to round depends on the purpose of the number, and closeness can be judged on a number line.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A news report says a football crowd was “about 54,000”. The exact number counted was 53,847. Is “about 54,000” a fair thing to report, or is it wrong because it isn't the exact number? How would you decide when a rounded number is good enough?' Surface the reasoning — don't grade it.
checkAnswer: Not scored. A rich response accepts that rounding is legitimate and useful, that 'about 54,000' fairly stands for 53,847 (nearest thousand), and that HOW MUCH to round depends on the purpose of the number.
